pos: n. (a freeman of a city, with its rights and duties — Greek polites)
etymology: Old French citeain, from Latin civitas, a city or commonwealth. The Greek polites is a member of the polis — one who belongs to the city and answers to it.
biblical_def: A citizen in Scripture is one who belongs to a commonwealth and holds its standing. The prodigal, having spent all, “joined himself to a citizen of that country; and he sent him into his fields to feed swine” (Luk 15:15) — a Jewish boy attached to a heathen householder and set to the most defiling work his own law knew. Paul claims the word for himself when the mob has him: “I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, a citizen of no mean city” (Act 21:39), and later claims his Roman citizenship to stop a scourging. Scripture nowhere despises civil standing; it is a real thing and a lawful protection. But it is not the standing that matters most. Paul writes to Gentiles, who had none: “Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God” (Eph 2:19). The word admits them to a commonwealth from which birth had excluded them. And he tells the church at Philippi, a Roman colony proud of its franchise, where their real registry lies: “For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Php 3:20) — the word behind conversation there is citizenship.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a citizen as the native of a city, or an inhabitant who enjoys the freedom and privileges of the city in which he resides; and in the United States, a person who enjoys the rights of a freeman.
webster_full: CIT'IZEN, n. The native of a city, or an inhabitant who enjoys the freedom and privileges of the city in which he resides.
2. A townsman; a man of trade; not a gentleman.
3. An inhabitant; a dweller in any city, town or place.
4. In the United States, a person, native or naturalized, who has the privilege of exercising the elective franchise.
scriptures: Ephesians 2:19
Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God;
Philippians 3:20
For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ:
Acts 21:39
But Paul said, I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, a citizen of no mean city: and, I beseech thee, suffer me to speak unto the people.
Luke 15:15
And he went and joined himself to a citizen of that country; and he sent him into his fields to feed swine.
corruption_summary: Earthly citizenship is made ultimate, or else despised altogether, and Scripture does neither: it uses civil standing without resting on it.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors face each other across this word. The first makes national belonging the deepest identity a man has, so that his politics organize his religion rather than the reverse. Philippians 3:20 was written to a Roman colony whose people were intensely proud of their franchise, and Paul told them their citizenship was in heaven. That does not abolish the earthly one — he used his own repeatedly, to stop a beating and to reach Caesar — but it settles the order. A Christian whose deepest loyalty is to a nation will eventually be asked by that nation to do something his Lord forbids, and will find he has no ground to stand on.

The second error withdraws from civil life as though it were beneath a heavenly citizen. Scripture gives no warrant. Paul insisted on his rights before magistrates; Daniel served an empire; Joseph administered Egypt; Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the peace of the city where they were carried. The believer is a resident with duties in the place God set him and a citizen of a better country he has not yet seen. Ephesians 2:19 is the promise that governs both: those who were strangers and foreigners have been made fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God — the household clause is what keeps the citizenship from being merely legal.

pos: n. (a man of rank; in John, a king's officer — Greek basilikos, one belonging to the king)
etymology: From noble, Latin nobilis, well known, and man. The Greek basilikos means royal — a man of the king's household or service.
biblical_def: The nobleman of John 4 is a courtier of Herod whose son lay dying at Capernaum. He came the twenty miles to Cana: “there was a certain nobleman, whose son was sick at Capernaum” (Joh 4:46), and when the Lord tested him — except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe — he did not argue: “Sir, come down ere my child die” (Joh 4:49). What he received was not what he asked. He asked the Lord to come; the Lord stayed where He was and spoke: “Go thy way; thy son liveth. And the man believed the word that Jesus had spoken unto him, and he went his way” (Joh 4:50). He walked home on a sentence. His servants met him with the news, and the fever had left the boy at the seventh hour, the hour Jesus spoke. A man of rank, accustomed to bringing physicians to the patient, learned that the word of Christ needs no journey. The other nobleman in the Gospels is in a parable: “A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom, and to return” (Luk 19:12) — the Lord's own picture of His departure, His coronation, and His return to reckon with the servants He left holding His money.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a nobleman as a man who belongs to the nobility; one who is noble by descent or by patent; a peer.
webster_full: NO'BLEMAN, n. A man who belongs to the nobility; one who is noble by descent or by patent; a peer.
NO'BLE, a. Great; elevated; dignified; illustrious; of high rank or birth.
COUR'TIER, n. One who attends or frequents the courts of princes.
RETINUE, n. The attendants of a prince or person of distinction.
scriptures: John 4:46
So Jesus came again into Cana of Galilee, where he made the water wine. And there was a certain nobleman, whose son was sick at Capernaum.
John 4:49
The nobleman saith unto him, Sir, come down ere my child die.
John 4:50
Jesus saith unto him, Go thy way; thy son liveth. And the man believed the word that Jesus had spoken unto him, and he went his way.
Luke 19:12
He said therefore, A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom, and to return.
corruption_summary: Faith is judged by the presence of feeling or of visible confirmation, when John records a man who believed a sentence and walked twenty miles home on it.
corruption_paragraphs: John 4:50 defines faith better than most treatises: the man believed the word that Jesus had spoken unto him, and he went his way. He had asked for a visit and received a sentence; he had no sign, no accompanying feeling recorded, and a day's walk in which to change his mind. He went. Where faith is defined as an experience, this man's conduct is unintelligible; where it is defined as taking God at His word, it is the pattern. And John adds the detail that made it verifiable: the servants named the hour, and the father knew it was the same hour in which Jesus spoke.

The parable in Luke 19 puts the same word to a use the church must not soften. The nobleman goes to receive a kingdom and to return, and his citizens send a message after him: we will not have this man to reign over us. The Lord told that parable on the road to Jerusalem, days before the crowds cried crucify him, and the return in the parable is a reckoning. Where the second coming is preached only as comfort, this parable is quietly dropped, since it ends with the servants audited and the rebels judged. Both are in it: rewards handed out by a Master delighted with faithfulness, and a settlement with those who refused His reign.

pos: n. (a woman of rank; in Isaiah, a title Babylon claimed — Hebrew gebereth; Greek kuria)
etymology: Old English hlæfdige, literally the loaf-kneader, the mistress of a household who distributed the bread. The Hebrew gebereth is a mistress or ruling woman; the Greek kuria is the feminine of kurios, lord.
biblical_def: Lady appears in the Authorized Version in two settings that could hardly be further apart. Isaiah addresses Babylon by the title she had taken: “Sit thou silent, and get thee into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called, The lady of kingdoms” (Isa 47:5), and names the presumption underneath it: “And thou saidst, I shall be a lady for ever: so that thou didst not lay these things to thy heart, neither didst remember the latter end of it” (Isa 47:7). Permanence assumed and the latter end unconsidered — that is the whole indictment of empires in one line. The other use is John's greeting: “The elder unto the elect lady and her children, whom I love in the truth; and not I only, but also all they that have known the truth” (2Jn 1:1), and “now I beseech thee, lady, not as though I wrote a new commandment unto thee, but that which we had from the beginning, that we love one another” (2Jn 1:5). An aged apostle writes a short letter to a Christian woman — or to a congregation addressed under that figure — about walking in truth, loving one another, and refusing hospitality to men who bring another doctrine. The lady of kingdoms is silenced; the elect lady is loved in the truth by all who know the truth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a lady as a woman of distinction; a title given to the wives of knights and of all degrees above them; and, in common usage, a well bred woman.
webster_full: LA'DY, n. A woman of distinction. Originally, the title was given to the daughters of earls and others in high rank, but it is now given to any well bred woman.
2. A word of complaisance; a well bred woman.
3. Mistress; the female who presides or has authority over a family or household.
MIS'TRESS, n. A woman who governs; correlative to servant or slave; the female head of a family.
scriptures: 2 John 1:1
The elder unto the elect lady and her children, whom I love in the truth; and not I only, but also all they that have known the truth;
2 John 1:5
And now I beseech thee, lady, not as though I wrote a new commandment unto thee, but that which we had from the beginning, that we love one another.
Isaiah 47:5
Sit thou silent, and get thee into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called, The lady of kingdoms.
Isaiah 47:7
And thou saidst, I shall be a lady for ever: so that thou didst not lay these things to thy heart, neither didst remember the latter end of it.
corruption_summary: Love and truth are set against each other, when the shortest letter in the New Testament joins them in every paragraph and then bars the door to false teachers.
corruption_paragraphs: Second John is four hundred words long and it says truth five times and love four, and never once sets them at odds. John loves the elect lady in the truth; he rejoices that her children walk in truth; he beseeches her that they love one another; and in the same breath he forbids her to receive into her house, or to bid God speed, anyone who brings not the doctrine of Christ. That last instruction is unbearable to a generation taught that love means unlimited welcome, and it comes from the apostle whom that same generation quotes on love. The letter is the standing proof that Christian love has a doctrinal shape and a door it will not open.

Isaiah 47 shows the other lady and her ruin. Babylon called herself the lady of kingdoms and said in her heart, I shall be a lady for ever, and the prophet fastens on what that boast made her stop doing: she did not lay these things to her heart, neither did she remember the latter end. Assumed permanence produces unconsidered ends, in an empire and in a soul. The remedy Moses prayed for is exactly the opposite: teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.

pos: n. (a betrothed or wedded companion; in the Song, the bride — Hebrew kallah)
etymology: Latin sponsa, a betrothed woman, from spondere, to promise solemnly. The Hebrew kallah means bride or daughter-in-law — a woman brought into a house by covenant.
biblical_def: Spouse in the Authorized Version belongs almost entirely to the Song of Solomon, where the bridegroom uses it repeatedly and never without an endearment attached. “Come with me from Lebanon, my spouse, with me from Lebanon: look from the top of Amana, from the top of Shenir and Hermon, from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards” (Son 4:8) — a call away from high and dangerous places to be with him. “Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one chain of thy neck” (Son 4:9). “How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse! how much better is thy love than wine!” (Son 4:10). The doubled title my sister, my spouse joins kinship and covenant: she is his by blood-nearness and by promise. The Song is first of all what it appears to be — the marriage of a man and a woman, given by God, praised without embarrassment — and Paul says of that very union that it signifies something further: “This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church” (Eph 5:32). The believer's standing is not that of a servant only. The church is a bride, called by name, delighted in, and told to come.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a spouse as a man or woman engaged or joined in wedlock; a married person, husband or wife; and also a person betrothed.
webster_full: SPOUSE, n. A man or woman engaged or joined in wedlock; a married person, husband or wife.
2. A person betrothed or promised in marriage.
BRIDE, n. A woman new married, or about to be married.
BETROTH', v.t. To contract to any one, in order to a future marriage; to promise or pledge in marriage.
scriptures: Song of Solomon 4:9
Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one chain of thy neck.
Song of Solomon 4:10
How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse! how much better is thy love than wine! and the smell of thine ointments than all spices!
Song of Solomon 4:8
Come with me from Lebanon, my spouse, with me from Lebanon: look from the top of Amana, from the top of Shenir and Hermon, from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards.
Ephesians 5:32
This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.
corruption_summary: Marriage is redefined as a contract of two consenting parties on any terms, and the Song is either allegorized until nothing bodily remains or read as though it were nothing else.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 5:32 makes marriage a sign, and a sign cannot be redefined by the parties who use it. Paul says the union of one man and one woman is a great mystery concerning Christ and the church; therefore its shape — one husband, one wife, covenanted for life, ordered in headship and in love — is not a social arrangement subject to revision but a picture God is using. To alter the picture is not to expand a human institution; it is to falsify a statement about Christ. That is why the church cannot treat the definition of marriage as a secondary matter, however costly it becomes to say so.

Two opposite errors have also plagued the reading of the Song itself. One allegorizes it so thoroughly that the woman disappears and every embrace becomes a doctrine, which cannot be right, since God gave the book its plain sense first and blessed the marriage bed without apology. The other refuses any further reference at all, which leaves the church without the Old Testament's richest vocabulary for the love of Christ toward His people — and Scripture itself will not allow it, since the prophets call the LORD Israel's husband and John sees the marriage supper of the Lamb. The Song is a real marriage, and a real marriage is a sign.

pos: n. (a married woman unfaithful to her husband — Hebrew naaph; Greek moichalis)
etymology: Latin adultera, from adulterare, to corrupt or falsify. The word names the falsifying of a covenant, not merely an act.
biblical_def: Adulteress names a woman who has broken the marriage covenant, and Scripture uses the word with equal weight upon the man. The law is explicit: “the man that committeth adultery with another man's wife, even he that committeth adultery with his neighbour's wife, the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death” (Lev 20:10) — both, in one sentence, with no double standard. Proverbs warns the young man of what it costs: “by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life” (Pro 6:26). Paul uses the term in a legal argument about the believer's release from the law: “if, while her husband liveth, she be married to another man, she shall be called an adulteress: but if her husband be dead, she is free from that law” (Rom 7:3). And Hosea receives the hardest command given to any prophet: “Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods, and love flagons of wine” (Hos 3:1). The comparison is stated by God Himself. Israel is the adulteress; the LORD is the husband who goes and buys her back. Every doctrine of covenant love in Scripture has to reckon with that chapter.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an adulteress as a married woman guilty of incontinence; and, in Scripture, an idolatress, or a soul unfaithful to God.
webster_full: ADUL'TERESS, n. A married woman guilty of incontinence.
ADUL'TERER, n. A man guilty of adultery; a man who has sexual commerce with any married woman, except his wife.
2. In Scripture, an idolater.
ADUL'TERY, n. Violation of the marriage bed; a crime, or a civil injury, which introduces confusion of progeny.
scriptures: Romans 7:3

So then if, while her husband liveth, she be married to another man, she shall be called an adulteress: but if her husband be dead, she is free from that law; so that she is no adulteress, though she be married to another man.
Hosea 3:1

Then said the LORD unto me, Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods, and love flagons of wine.
Leviticus 20:10
And the man that committeth adultery with another man's wife, even he that committeth adultery with his neighbour's wife, the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death.
Proverbs 6:26
For by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life.
corruption_summary: Adultery is reclassified as a private matter between consenting adults, and the covenant it breaks — along with the God who witnesses it — is left out of the accounting.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern reckoning treats adultery as a failure of a relationship rather than the breaking of a covenant, and therefore as a matter for the parties alone. Malachi answers directly: the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, and He hates putting away. A marriage in Scripture has three parties, and the third does not leave when the vows grow inconvenient. This is also why Proverbs speaks of the adulteress hunting for the precious life — the injury reaches past reputation and property into the soul, and both the man and the woman in the case are said to destroy their own.

Two guards must be set on this word. First, Scripture's standard is even-handed: Leviticus condemns the adulterer and the adulteress in one clause, and the Lord dealt far more sharply with the men who dragged a woman before Him than with her. A church that whispers about women and excuses men has not learned the law it claims to keep. Second, Hosea 3 forbids the conclusion that such a sinner is beyond love. God commanded a prophet to go and love an adulteress, buy her back at the price of a slave, and keep her — and said plainly that this was according to the love of the LORD toward Israel. The condemnation and the redemption are in the same Bible and often in the same chapter.

pos: n. pl. (female servants; in Joel and Acts, recipients of the outpoured Spirit — Hebrew shiphchah; Greek doule)
etymology: From hand and maiden — a maid at hand, a female attendant. The Hebrew and Greek words both mean bondwoman: the lowest rank in a household.
biblical_def: Handmaidens are bondwomen, the lowest servants of a house, and Scripture puts them at the centre of Pentecost. Peter quotes Joel: “And on my servants and on my handmaidens I will pour out in those days of my Spirit; and they shall prophesy” (Act 2:18). The prophecy names the classes the ancient world had least regard for — menservants and maidservants — and says the Spirit will be poured on them. In the Old Testament they appear as property: at the meeting with Esau, “the handmaidens came near, they and their children, and they bowed themselves” (Gen 33:6), sent first because they were valued least. Ruth, a Moabitess gleaning in a stranger's field, does not presume even to that rank: “Let me find favour in thy sight, my lord; for that thou hast comforted me, and for that thou hast spoken friendly unto thine handmaid, though I be not like unto one of thine handmaidens” (Rut 2:13). And the word is taken up as a title of honour by the mother of the Lord: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word” (Luk 1:38). Told that she would bear the Son of God, Mary answered by naming herself a bondwoman and consenting to His word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a handmaid or handmaiden as a maid that waits at hand; a female servant or attendant.
webster_full: HANDMAID, HANDMAIDEN, n. A maid that waits at hand; a female servant or attendant.
MAID'EN, n. An unmarried woman, or a young unmarried woman; a virgin.
BOND'WOMAN, n. A woman slave; a female in bondage.
SERV'ANT, n. A person, male or female, that attends another for the purpose of performing menial offices for him.
scriptures: Acts 2:18
And on my servants and on my handmaidens I will pour out in those days of my Spirit; and they shall prophesy:
Luke 1:38
And Mary said, Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word. And the angel departed from her.
Genesis 33:6
Then the handmaidens came near, they and their children, and they bowed themselves.
Ruth 2:13

Then she said, Let me find favour in thy sight, my lord; for that thou hast comforted me, and for that thou hast spoken friendly unto thine handmaid, though I be not like unto one of thine handmaidens.
corruption_summary: Acts 2:18 is pressed to overturn the order of the church, and it is equally mishandled by those who quietly pass over the women it names.
corruption_paragraphs: Joel's prophecy, quoted by Peter, says the Spirit is poured on servants and handmaidens and that they shall prophesy. It is regularly enlisted to abolish the male eldership, and it does not reach the question. Prophesying is not the pastoral office; Philip's four daughters prophesied, and the same book of Acts and the same apostolic writings appoint elders who are to be the husband of one wife, apt to teach, ruling their own houses well. The Spirit's gifts are distributed to whom He will; the offices of the church are fixed by Christ's appointment, and neither cancels the other.

The opposite mishandling is more common in conservative churches and deserves naming plainly. The text says handmaidens, and it says the Spirit was poured out on them, and Luke records women in the upper room, women at the tomb first, women labouring with Paul in the gospel, and Priscilla instructing Apollos in her home. A congregation that reads Joel 2 and hears only the sons has abbreviated the verse. The order Scripture gives is not a ranking of worth — Mary's be it unto me according to thy word is the finest single act of faith recorded in the Gospels, and it was spoken by a young woman who called herself a bondwoman.

pos: n. (one who takes on loan; in Proverbs, the lender's servant — Hebrew lavah, to borrow)
etymology: From borrow, Old English borgian, to give a pledge. The Hebrew lavah means to join or attach — a borrower is bound to his lender.
biblical_def: The borrower in Scripture is a man whose freedom has been reduced. Solomon states it without qualification: “The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender” (Pro 22:7). It is a proverb, not a prohibition — the law permitted lending and regulated it strictly — but it is a plain statement of what debt does. A borrower has sold a portion of his future obedience; his time, his labour, and often his conscience are now attached to another man's claim. Isaiah uses the pair to picture a levelling judgment in which every station is swept alike: “as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the taker of usury, so with the giver of usury to him” (Isa 24:2). The Psalmist names the moral failure that turns borrowing into sin: “The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous sheweth mercy, and giveth” (Psa 37:21) — the wickedness is in the not repaying. And Paul gives the apostolic rule, with its one permanent exception: “Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law” (Rom 13:8). One debt is to be kept perpetually outstanding, and it is not financial.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a borrower as one who borrows; one who takes what belongs to another to use for a time, and to return, or an equivalent.
webster_full: BOR'ROWER, n. One who borrows; opposed to lender.
BOR'ROW, v.t. To take from another by request and consent, with a view to use the thing taken for a time, and return it, or something equivalent.
LEND'ER, n. One who lends; one who makes a trade of putting money to interest.
US'URY, n. Formerly, interest; a premium given for the use of money; now, unlawful interest, or a premium beyond the rate established by law.
scriptures: Proverbs 22:7
The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender.
Psalm 37:21
The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous sheweth mercy, and giveth.
Romans 13:8
Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law.
Isaiah 24:2

And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the taker of usury, so with the giver of usury to him.
corruption_summary: Debt is treated as a neutral financial instrument, and the servitude Proverbs names is not counted as a cost at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 22:7 states a fact that no arrangement can repeal: the borrower is servant to the lender. Modern credit is presented purely as access — a house sooner, an education, a business begun — and the servitude clause is nowhere in the offer. Scripture does not forbid borrowing, and it commands lending to the poor without interest, so this is not a rule but a warning about a price that is real whether or not it is disclosed. A man deep in debt is not free to move, to give, to take a lower-paying calling, or in some cases to speak, and every one of those constraints is a form of the service Solomon named.

Two balancing truths keep the entry honest. Psalm 37:21 locates the wickedness precisely: the wicked borroweth, and payeth not again. The sin is the default, not the loan, and a Christian who borrows takes on a debt of honour to repay it. And Romans 13:8 leaves one obligation deliberately unpaid: owe no man any thing, but to love one another. The apostle uses the language of debt to describe love because love is the one account that is never settled — a believer is always in arrears to his neighbour, and always to be paying.
roots_summary: Hebrew lavah (H3867), to join, and so to borrow or lend — Proverbs 22:7, Psalm 37:21, Deuteronomy 28:12; nashak (H5391), to bite, to lend on usury.
roots_lines: Hebrew lavah (H3867) — to join oneself, to borrow or lend; Proverbs 22:7, Psalm 37:21, Deuteronomy 28:12.
Hebrew nashak (H5391) — to bite, and so to lend on interest; Deuteronomy 23:19, Exodus 22:25.
Hebrew abat (H5670) — to lend on pledge; Deuteronomy 15:6 and 15:8, of lending to the poor brother.
Deuteronomy 15 required the release of debts in the seventh year, and forbade a hard eye toward a brother in need as that year approached.
Romans 13:8 keeps one debt permanently open: to love one another.
usage: “The borrower is servant to the lender” — a fact, not a prohibition.
“The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again” — the sin is the default.
“Owe no man any thing, but to love one another” — the account never settled.

pos: n. (alliance by marriage; kinship contracted rather than born — Hebrew chathan, to make oneself a son-in-law)
etymology: Latin affinitas, relation by marriage, from ad and finis, a border — those whose lands, and so whose houses, adjoin. The Hebrew verb means to become a son-in-law by marriage.
biblical_def: Affinity in Scripture is alliance made by marriage, and every occurrence is a warning. Solomon's reign opens with it: “Solomon made affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt, and took Pharaoh's daughter, and brought her into the city of David” (1Ki 3:1) — recorded before the dream at Gibeon and the wisdom, and the seed of the wives who turned away his heart in his old age. Jehoshaphat, a good king, made the same mistake with a worse man: “Now Jehoshaphat had riches and honour in abundance, and joined affinity with Ahab” (2Ch 18:1). The next verse takes him to Ramothgilead in Ahab's chariot, where a prophet asks him why he helps the ungodly, and his son later marries Athaliah, who murders the royal seed. Ezra, in the great confession, states the principle: “Should we again break thy commandments, and join in affinity with the people of these abominations? wouldest not thou be angry with us till thou hadst consumed us, so that there should be no remnant nor escaping?” (Ezr 9:14). Paul's rule is the same in the New Covenant: “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness?” (2Co 6:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines affinity as the relation contracted by marriage between a husband and his wife's kindred; distinguished from consanguinity, which is relation by blood.
webster_full: AFFIN'ITY, n. The relation contracted by marriage, between a husband and his wife's kindred, and between a wife and her husband's kindred; in contradistinction from consanguinity or relation by blood.
2. Agreement; relation; conformity; resemblance; connection.
3. In chemistry, the attraction which takes place between the particles of substances of different kinds.
CONSANGUIN'ITY, n. The relation of persons by blood; kindred by birth.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 18:1
Now Jehoshaphat had riches and honour in abundance, and joined affinity with Ahab.
1 Kings 3:1

And Solomon made affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt, and took Pharaoh's daughter, and brought her into the city of David, until he had made an end of building his own house, and the house of the LORD, and the wall of Jerusalem round about.
Ezra 9:14

Should we again break thy commandments, and join in affinity with the people of these abominations? wouldest not thou be angry with us till thou hadst consumed us, so that there should be no remnant nor escaping?
2 Corinthians 6:14
Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?
corruption_summary: Alliance with what God has separated from is defended as strategy, influence, or generosity, and the ruin it brings arrives a generation later when no one connects the two.
corruption_paragraphs: The narratives are unusually clear about the delay. Solomon's affinity with Egypt is recorded at the beginning of a reign of unmatched glory; the harvest — wives who turned away his heart, high places for Chemosh and Molech, a kingdom torn in two — comes many chapters later. Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahab looks like statesmanship; the fruit is his son's marriage to Athaliah and the near extinction of the house of David. Compromise is judged by what it produces at length, and it almost never produces it soon enough for the man who made it to be warned by it.

Paul's rule in 2 Corinthians 6:14 must be handled with the same care Scripture uses. It is not a command to withdraw from unbelievers — Paul says explicitly elsewhere that this would require going out of the world, and Christians are to eat with them, work with them, and be blameless among them. The yoke is the binding partnership: marriage first of all, and any alliance in which a believer's course is set by an unbeliever's aims. Ezra's question is the one to ask of any such union: should we again break thy commandments? The word again is the point — he was speaking to a people who had already been consumed once for it.
roots_summary: Hebrew chathan (H2859), to become a son-in-law, make affinity — 1 Kings 3:1, 2 Chronicles 18:1, Ezra 9:14, Deuteronomy 7:3; Greek heterozugeo (G2086), to be unequally yoked.
roots_lines: Hebrew chathan (H2859) — to make oneself a son-in-law, to contract affinity; 1 Kings 3:1, 2 Chronicles 18:1, Ezra 9:14.
Hebrew chathan as a noun — a bridegroom or son-in-law; the same root, which is why marriage is the whole idea.
Greek heterozugeo (G2086) — to be yoked with one of another kind; 2 Corinthians 6:14, its only occurrence.
Deuteronomy 7:3 gives the original prohibition, and states the reason in verse 4: they will turn away thy son from following me.
Every occurrence of the word in Scripture is followed, sooner or later, by trouble for the house that made it.
usage: “Joined affinity with Ahab” — and the fruit came a generation later.
“Should we again break thy commandments” — Ezra's word is again.
“Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers”.

pos: adj. (lower in place, rank or worth — Latin inferior, lower)
etymology: Latin inferior, the comparative of inferus, low. The Hebrew idiom in Job 12:3 is literally I fall not lower than you.
biblical_def: Inferior means lower, and the Authorized Version uses it in three registers. Job protests against comforters who spoke to him as to a simpleton: “I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you: yea, who knoweth not such things as these?” (Job 12:3), and again, “What ye know, the same do I know also: I am not inferior unto you” (Job 13:2). His complaint is not vanity; it is that they were reciting commonplaces to a man in agony as though he had never heard them. Daniel uses the word of empires: “after thee shall arise another kingdom inferior to thee, and another third kingdom of brass, which shall bear rule over all the earth” (Dan 2:39) — the great image descends in value from head to feet, gold to silver to brass to iron and clay, and every kingdom of men is on that descending scale until a stone cut without hands breaks them all. And Paul uses it with heavy irony toward a church that had begun to despise him: “For what is it wherein ye were inferior to other churches, except it be that I myself was not burdensome to you? forgive me this wrong” (2Co 12:13). The one respect in which Corinth had less than other churches was that their apostle had refused to take their money.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inferior as lower in place, station, age, value or excellence; subordinate; of less importance or worth.
webster_full: INFE'RIOR, a. Lower in place; as the inferior limbs.
2. Lower in station, age, or rank in life; as a person of inferior rank.
3. Lower in excellence or value; as a poem of inferior merit.
INFERIOR'ITY, n. A lower state of dignity, value, or amount.
scriptures: Job 13:2
What ye know, the same do I know also: I am not inferior unto you.
Job 12:3
But I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you: yea, who knoweth not such things as these?
Daniel 2:39
And after thee shall arise another kingdom inferior to thee, and another third kingdom of brass, which shall bear rule over all the earth.
2 Corinthians 12:13
For what is it wherein ye were inferior to other churches, except it be that I myself was not burdensome to you? forgive me this wrong.
corruption_summary: Rank and worth are confused, so that a difference of office or gift is read as a difference of value before God.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture distinguishes order from worth at every level, and losing the distinction produces error in both directions. There are inferior and superior kingdoms in Daniel, real subordination in a household and in a church, and a real hierarchy of gifts — and there is one price paid for every soul, one Spirit given, one inheritance. Paul's argument about the body makes the point exactly: the members that seem to be more feeble are necessary, and God has given more abundant honour to the part that lacked. A man convinced that his place makes him inferior in worth has misread the body; a man who thinks his place makes him superior has misread it in the other direction and more dangerously.

Job's use of the word rebukes a particular pastoral failure. His friends were saying true things — much of what they said would be sound in another mouth on another day — and they said them to a man on an ash heap as though he needed instruction in the ABC of religion. Who knoweth not such things as these? The failure was not their doctrine but their contempt, and God's verdict at the end of the book fell on them, not on Job. And Paul's irony in 2 Corinthians 12:13 exposes the strangest version of it: a congregation valuing its apostle less because he would not charge them.
roots_summary: Aramaic ara (H772), lower, inferior — Daniel 2:39; Hebrew naphal (H5307), to fall, in the idiom I fall not lower than you — Job 12:3; Greek hettaomai (G2274), to be made worse or inferior — 2 Corinthians 12:13.
roots_lines: Aramaic ara (H772) — lower, inferior; Daniel 2:39, of the kingdom after Babylon.
Hebrew naphal (H5307) — to fall; Job 12:3, whose margin reads I fall not lower than you.
Greek hettaomai (G2274) — to be made inferior, worsted; 2 Corinthians 12:13, 2 Peter 2:19-20.
Daniel 2 descends from gold to iron and clay, and the stone cut without hands breaks them all.
1 Corinthians 12:23-24 sets the rule for the body: more abundant honour given to the part that lacked.
usage: “I am not inferior unto you” — said to comforters reciting commonplaces.
“Another kingdom inferior to thee” — the image descends all the way down.
“Except it be that I myself was not burdensome to you? forgive me this wrong”.

pos: adj. (leagued together by covenant — Hebrew baal berith, lords of a covenant; nuach, to rest upon)
etymology: Latin confoederatus, from con- and foedus, a league or treaty. To be confederate is to be bound to others by a compact.
biblical_def: Confederate means bound in league, and Scripture shows three kinds. There is the lawful alliance of neighbours: Abram dwelt in the plain of Mamre the Amorite, “brother of Eshcol, and brother of Aner: and these were confederate with Abram” (Gen 14:13), and they went with him to recover Lot. There is the conspiracy of the nations against God: “For they have consulted together with one consent: they are confederate against thee” (Psa 83:5) — and the psalm lists ten peoples joined for one purpose, to cut off Israel from being a nation. And there is the alliance that terrifies: “it was told the house of David, saying, Syria is confederate with Ephraim. And his heart was moved, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind” (Isa 7:2). Two kingdoms had leagued against Judah and the court shook like a forest in a gale. God's answer to Ahaz was the sign of Immanuel, and His answer to the people came a chapter later: “Say ye not, A confederacy, to all them to whom this people shall say, A confederacy; neither fear ye their fear, nor be afraid” (Isa 8:12). Do not adopt the fear of the fearful, nor join the panic-alliances that fear produces.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines confederate as united in a league; allied by treaty; and, as a noun, one who is united with others in a league or compact.
webster_full: CONFED'ERATE, a. United in a league; allied by treaty; engaged in a confederacy.
CONFED'ERATE, n. One who is united with others in a league; a person or nation engaged in a confederacy; an ally.
CONFED'ERACY, n. A league, or covenant; a contract between two or more persons, bodies of men or states, combined in support of each other.
LEAGUE, n. An alliance or confederacy between princes or states, for their mutual aid or defense.
scriptures: Genesis 14:13
And there came one that had escaped, and told Abram the Hebrew; for he dwelt in the plain of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol, and brother of Aner: and these were confederate with Abram.
Psalm 83:5
For they have consulted together with one consent: they are confederate against thee:
Isaiah 7:2
And it was told the house of David, saying, Syria is confederate with Ephraim. And his heart was moved, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind.
Isaiah 8:12
Say ye not, A confederacy, to all them to whom this people shall say, A confederacy; neither fear ye their fear, nor be afraid.
corruption_summary: Fear drives the people of God into alliances they were never authorized to make, and Isaiah 8:12 forbids both the panic and the leagues it produces.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 8:12 is one of the most practical verses in the prophets and one of the least applied. Judah was in genuine danger; Syria and Ephraim really were leagued against her; and God told His people not to say a confederacy along with everyone else, nor to fear their fear. The prohibition is against catching the alarm of the crowd and against the reflexive alliance-making that alarm produces. Ahaz did not heed it: he sent silver and gold to the king of Assyria and said, I am thy servant, and the empire he bought protection from later ground his kingdom down. A frightened church makes bargains it would never make in a settled hour, and pays for them for generations.

Psalm 83 shows the other side and keeps the entry from becoming mere caution. Ten nations consulted together with one consent and were confederate against thee — the psalmist takes the whole coalition and hands it to God, and the psalm is a prayer, not a strategy. That is what a believing people does with a confederacy it cannot break. Genesis 14 shows that lawful alliances exist: Abram had neighbours who were confederate with him and who went to war beside him, and he took no spoil from the king of Sodom afterwards, lest that man should say he had made Abram rich. Alliance, yes; obligation to the ungodly, no.
roots_summary: Hebrew baal berith, lords of a covenant — Genesis 14:13; karath berith, to cut a covenant — Psalm 83:5; nuach (H5117), to rest upon, of Syria resting on Ephraim — Isaiah 7:2; qesher (H7195), a conspiracy — Isaiah 8:12.
roots_lines: Hebrew berith (H1285) — a covenant; the root idea in every confederacy, lawful or not.
Hebrew nuach (H5117) — to rest, settle upon; Isaiah 7:2, literally Syria resteth upon Ephraim.
Hebrew qesher (H7195) — a conspiracy, league; Isaiah 8:12, and of the conspiracies against the kings of Judah.
Psalm 83:6-8 names the ten confederate peoples, from Edom and Ishmael to Assur, joined against Israel.
Isaiah 8:13 gives the alternative to fearing a confederacy: sanctify the LORD of hosts himself, and let him be your fear.
usage: “These were confederate with Abram” — a lawful alliance of neighbours.
“They are confederate against thee” — the coalition handed to God in prayer.
“Say ye not, A confederacy… neither fear ye their fear”.

pos: adj. (pertaining to the flesh; carnal, as opposed to spiritual — Greek sarkikos)
etymology: From flesh, Old English flæsc. The Greek sarkikos means belonging to the flesh — not the body as created, but the fallen nature considered as a principle of action.
biblical_def: Fleshly describes what proceeds from the fallen nature rather than from the Spirit, and Scripture applies it to three things a man might not suspect. To desires: “Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul” (1Pe 2:11) — and note that the war is against the soul, not merely against the body. To wisdom: “our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world” (2Co 1:12) — there is a cleverness in ministry that is of the flesh, and Paul renounces it. And, most surprisingly, to religion: “Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind” (Col 2:18). The man described there is ascetic, humble in appearance, absorbed in things unseen — and Paul calls his mind fleshly. That is the sting of the word. The flesh is not merely appetite; it is self operating in any mode, including the devout one, and Paul says such observances have no value against the indulgence of the flesh. The conflict is permanent this side of glory: “the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh” (Gal 5:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fleshly as pertaining to the flesh; carnal; not spiritual; animal; as fleshly lusts.
webster_full: FLESH'LY, a. Pertaining to the flesh; corporeal.
2. Carnal; worldly; lascivious; as fleshly lusts.
3. Human; not celestial; not spiritual or divine.
CAR'NAL, a. Fleshly; pertaining to flesh; not spiritual; opposed to spiritual or regenerate.
scriptures: 1 Peter 2:11
Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;
2 Corinthians 1:12

For our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and more abundantly to you-ward.
Colossians 2:18
Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind,
Galatians 5:17
For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would.
corruption_summary: The flesh is identified with the body, so that the sins of the mind and of religion itself escape the category entirely, and asceticism is mistaken for mortification.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest mistake with this word is to equate flesh with body and therefore to locate all fleshly sin below the neck. Colossians 2:18 destroys that reading in a phrase: vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind. The man in view is not a glutton; he is an ascetic with visions, practising voluntary humility and worshipping angels, and Paul calls his mind fleshly and says his observances are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh. Pride, faction, self-display in devotion, and religious cleverness are all works of the flesh, and Galatians 5 lists hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions and heresies beside drunkenness in one catalogue.

The ancient error was to conclude that the body itself is the problem, and it has never fully left the church. Scripture teaches otherwise: God made the body, the Son took one, the Spirit indwells it as a temple, and it will be raised. What is condemned is not matter but the fallen nature that uses body and mind alike for its own ends. Hence Peter's warning that fleshly lusts war against the soul. The damage is not chiefly bodily and the remedy is not chiefly bodily either: it is walking in the Spirit, which is the one thing Galatians promises will keep a man from fulfilling the lust of the flesh.
roots_summary: Greek sarkikos (G4559), fleshly, carnal — 1 Peter 2:11, 2 Corinthians 1:12, Romans 15:27; sarx (G4561), flesh; psuchikos (G5591), natural or soulish.
roots_lines: Greek sarkikos (G4559) — fleshly, carnal; 1 Peter 2:11, 2 Corinthians 1:12, 2 Corinthians 10:4 of weapons not carnal.
Greek sarx (G4561) — flesh; used of the body, of human nature, and of the fallen principle of action.
Greek psuchikos (G5591) — natural, soulish; 1 Corinthians 2:14 of the natural man who receiveth not the things of the Spirit.
Colossians 2:23 states the verdict on fleshly religion: not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.
Galatians 5:19-21 lists the works of the flesh, and most of the items are not bodily appetites.
usage: “Fleshly lusts, which war against the soul” — the war is not merely bodily.
“Not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God” — cleverness renounced.
“Vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind” — said of an ascetic.

pos: n. pl. (first principles, rudiments; also the constituent stuff of the heavens — Greek stoicheia)
etymology: Latin elementum, a first principle. The Greek stoicheia means things in a row — the ABC, the rudiments; and by extension the basic constituents of the physical order.
biblical_def: Elements renders a Greek word meaning rudiments — the ABC of a subject — and Paul uses it of the state of the church before Christ came. “Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world” (Gal 4:3). The old covenant order of days, months, times and years was a schoolmaster: real, God-given, and elementary. To return to it after Christ is therefore not conservatism but regression: “now, after that ye have known God, or rather are known of God, how turn ye again to the weak and beggarly elements, whereunto ye desire again to be in bondage?” (Gal 4:9). The adjectives are severe — weak, because ceremonies cannot justify; beggarly, because they have nothing left to give once the substance has come. Peter uses the same word of the physical creation at the end: “the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up” (2Pe 3:10), and again, “the heavens being on fire shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat” (2Pe 3:12). The rudiments of religion are outgrown in Christ; the elements of the world are dissolved at His coming.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines element as the first or constituent principle of any thing; the simplest part; and in the plural, the rudiments or first principles of any art or science.
webster_full: EL'EMENT, n. The first or constituent principle or minutest part of any thing.
2. An ingredient; a constituent part of any substance.
3. In the plural, the first rules or principles of an art or science; rudiments.
RU'DIMENT, n. A first principle or element; that which is to be first learnt.
scriptures: Galatians 4:3
Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world:
Galatians 4:9
But now, after that ye have known God, or rather are known of God, how turn ye again to the weak and beggarly elements, whereunto ye desire again to be in bondage?
2 Peter 3:10

But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up.
2 Peter 3:12
Looking for and hasting unto the coming of the day of God, wherein the heavens being on fire shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat?
corruption_summary: The ceremonies Christ fulfilled are reimposed as marks of seriousness, and the promised dissolution of the present order is quietly dropped as embarrassing.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 4 is aimed at people who thought they were advancing. They were adding observances, taking on discipline, becoming more rigorous — and Paul says they were turning again to weak and beggarly elements and desiring to be in bondage. The pattern recurs whenever a church treats ceremony, calendar, dietary rule or ascetic practice as the mark of a serious Christian. Those things were the alphabet; Christ is the language. To go back to the alphabet after learning to read is not devotion. Paul's alarm in this epistle — I am afraid of you, lest I have bestowed upon you labour in vain — is proportioned to what is at stake, which he says elsewhere is falling from grace.

Second Peter 3 is dropped for the opposite reason: it is too concrete. The heavens passing away with a great noise, the elements melting with fervent heat, the earth and its works burned up — this is not the language of a symbol, and it is regularly softened into one. Peter draws two conclusions and neither is speculative. First, since all these things shall be dissolved, what manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness. Second, we look for new heavens and a new earth wherein dwelleth righteousness. The dissolution is not the end of the story; it is the clearing of the ground.
roots_summary: Greek stoicheia (G4747), rudiments, first principles, and the constituent elements of the world — Galatians 4:3, 4:9, Colossians 2:8, 2:20, Hebrews 5:12, 2 Peter 3:10, 3:12.
roots_lines: Greek stoicheion (G4747) — a rudiment or element; Galatians 4:3 and 4:9, Colossians 2:8 and 2:20, Hebrews 5:12, 2 Peter 3:10 and 3:12.
Greek ptochos (G4434) — beggarly, destitute; Galatians 4:9, of the elements returned to.
Greek luo (G3089) — to loose, dissolve; 2 Peter 3:10-12 of the elements melting.
Hebrews 5:12 uses the word of the first principles of the oracles of God, which the readers needed taught again.
The same word covers the ABC of religion and the constituent stuff of the heavens; both are provisional.
usage: “In bondage under the elements of the world” — the alphabet, before the language.
“How turn ye again to the weak and beggarly elements?”
“The elements shall melt with fervent heat” — and then, what manner of persons ought ye to be.

pos: v.i. (to disappear; to pass out of being — Greek aphanizo and katargeo)
etymology: Latin evanescere, to pass away, from vanus, empty. To vanish is to become vanus — to be emptied out of existence.
biblical_def: Vanish in Scripture is used of what will not last, and the list is startling. Of the heavens: “Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look upon the earth beneath: for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment… but my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished” (Isa 51:6). Of the gifts of the Spirit: “Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away” (1Co 13:8). Of the old covenant: “In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old. Now that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away” (Heb 8:13). And of a man's life: “ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away” (Jas 4:14). Job uses it of friends who fail like a summer brook: what time they wax warm, they vanish. Four things named as vanishing — the sky, spiritual gifts, the first covenant, and human life — and against them Isaiah sets one thing that does not: my salvation shall be for ever.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vanish as to disappear; to pass from a visible to an invisible state; to pass away; to be annihilated or lost.
webster_full: VAN'ISH, v.i. To disappear; to pass from a visible to an invisible state; as, vapor vanishes from the sight.
2. To disappear; to pass away; to be annihilated or lost; as, a cloud vanishes.
3. To pass beyond the limit of vision; as, the ship vanished from sight.
VA'POR, n. In a general sense, an invisible fluid; any thing unsubstantial or transitory.
scriptures: Hebrews 8:13
In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old. Now that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away.
1 Corinthians 13:8
Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away.
Isaiah 51:6

Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look upon the earth beneath: for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment, and they that dwell therein shall die in like manner: but my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished.
James 4:14
Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.
corruption_summary: The permanence of the wrong things is assumed — the present world, a man's own span, and gifts that were given for a season — and the one thing said to last for ever is treated as the uncertainty.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 51:6 puts the whole matter in one verse and reverses the ordinary reckoning. The sky is the standing figure of permanence in every language, and the prophet says it will vanish like smoke; the earth will wear out like a garment; the men on it will die. Then: but my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished. Most men live as though the arrangement were the other way round — the world solid, the salvation speculative — and every decision about how to spend a life is finally made on that reckoning, whether or not it is ever examined.

James 4:14 makes the same point at the scale of one man, and it is aimed at planners: we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain. James does not forbid planning; he forbids planning without God, and prescribes the corrective phrase — if the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that. And Hebrews 8:13 applies the word to the old covenant, written when the temple was still standing and the sacrifices still smoking: that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away. Within a few years it was gone. What God has said is passing is passing, however permanent it looks on the morning.
roots_summary: Greek aphanizo (G853), to make unseen, cause to vanish — James 4:14, Matthew 6:19; katargeo (G2673), to render inoperative, do away — 1 Corinthians 13:8; aphanismos (G854), disappearance — Hebrews 8:13.
roots_lines: Greek aphanizo (G853) — to make unseen, disfigure, cause to vanish; James 4:14, Matthew 6:19 of moth and rust.
Greek katargeo (G2673) — to make of no effect, do away with; 1 Corinthians 13:8, 2 Corinthians 3:11 of the glory that was to be done away.
Greek aphanismos (G854) — vanishing, disappearance; Hebrews 8:13, its only occurrence.
Hebrew malach (H4414) — to vanish away as smoke; Isaiah 51:6.
Isaiah 51:6 sets the one exception against the four vanishings: my salvation shall be for ever.
usage: “The heavens shall vanish away like smoke… but my salvation shall be for ever”.
“That which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away”.
“What is your life? It is even a vapour” — and James is writing to planners.

pos: adj. (before the due season; of a birth or a fig that drops unripe — Hebrew nephel; Greek olunthos)
etymology: From un- and timely. The Hebrew nephel is from the verb to fall — a birth that falls before its time; the Greek olunthos is the unripe winter fig that drops when the tree is shaken.
biblical_def: Untimely means before the appointed season, and Scripture uses it of two things that fall too soon. Of a birth: Job, in the depth of his misery, wishes he had been “as an hidden untimely birth… as infants which never saw light” (Job 3:16); the Psalmist prays against the wicked, “like the untimely birth of a woman, that they may not see the sun” (Psa 58:8); and the Preacher says that a man who has a hundred children and many years, whose soul is not filled with good and who has no burial, is worse off than an untimely birth (Ecc 6:3). In every case the phrase carries a weight of grief that Scripture does not minimize. Of fruit: at the sixth seal, “the stars of heaven fell unto the earth, even as a fig tree casteth her untimely figs, when she is shaken of a mighty wind” (Rev 6:13). Anyone who has seen a fig tree in a gale knows the picture — the small hard winter figs come down all at once, in a shower, because they were never fastened. That is John's image for the shaking of the heavens: what looked fixed comes down like unripe fruit when the wind rises.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines untimely as happening before the natural time; premature; and as an adverb, before the natural time.
webster_full: UNTI'MELY, a. Happening before the natural time; premature; as untimely fruit; an untimely death.
UNTI'MELY, adv. Before the natural time.
PREMATU'RE, a. Ripe too soon; too early; happening or performed before the proper time.
FIG, n. The fruit of the fig tree; the winter or untimely fig, which drops unripe.
scriptures: Revelation 6:13
And the stars of heaven fell unto the earth, even as a fig tree casteth her untimely figs, when she is shaken of a mighty wind.
Ecclesiastes 6:3

If a man beget an hundred children, and live many years, so that the days of his years be many, and his soul be not filled with good, and also that he have no burial; I say, that an untimely birth is better than he.
Job 3:16
Or as an hidden untimely birth I had not been; as infants which never saw light.
Psalm 58:8
As a snail which melteth, let every one of them pass away: like the untimely birth of a woman, that they may not see the sun.
corruption_summary: Grief that God recorded without rebuke is treated as unbelief, and the reader is left with no permission to say what Job said.
corruption_paragraphs: Job 3 is one of the darkest chapters in the Bible: a righteous man cursing the day of his birth and wishing he had been an untimely birth that never saw light. God preserved it in Scripture, and when He finally answered Job out of the whirlwind, He did not rebuke him for that chapter — He rebuked the friends who had spoken of Him wrongly, and told them to ask Job to pray for them. A church that permits its people no lament has less room in it than the Bible does. The Psalms are full of the same speech, and Christ Himself prayed one of them from the cross.

Ecclesiastes 6:3 measures a life by an unexpected standard. A hundred children and a long span, and yet a soul not filled with good and no burial at the end — and the Preacher says an untimely birth is better. That is a verdict on the accumulation of years and offspring and estate without God; the length is not the measure. Revelation 6:13 supplies the counterpart at the scale of the cosmos. When the mighty wind comes, what falls first is what was never firmly attached, and it falls all at once. The question the image asks a reader is not when the shaking comes but what he is fastened to.
roots_summary: Hebrew nephel (H5309), an untimely birth, from naphal, to fall — Job 3:16, Psalm 58:8, Ecclesiastes 6:3; Greek olunthos (G3653), the unripe winter fig — Revelation 6:13 only.
roots_lines: Hebrew nephel (H5309) — an untimely birth; Job 3:16, Psalm 58:8, Ecclesiastes 6:3, its only three occurrences.
Hebrew naphal (H5307) — to fall; the root, so the noun names a falling before the season.
Greek olunthos (G3653) — the unripe fig of winter; Revelation 6:13, its only occurrence.
Greek seio (G4579) — to shake; the mighty wind that brings the figs down.
Job 42:7-8 records that God's anger was kindled against the friends, not against the man who spoke Job 3.
usage: “As a fig tree casteth her untimely figs” — what was never fastened comes down first.
“An untimely birth is better than he” — length is not the measure of a life.
God preserved Job 3 in Scripture and did not rebuke it.

pos: n. (that which sustains life; food and provision — Hebrew michyah; Greek chortasma)
etymology: Latin sustinere, to hold up, sustain. Sustenance is not luxury but what holds a life up — the daily minimum.
biblical_def: Sustenance is what keeps a life standing, and Scripture shows it removed, supplied, and asked for. Removed: under Midian, the invaders “encamped against them, and destroyed the increase of the earth, till thou come unto Gaza, and left no sustenance for Israel, neither sheep, nor ox, nor ass” (Jdg 6:4), and it was out of that famine that God called Gideon threshing wheat by the winepress to hide it. Stephen recounts the same in Egypt: “there came a dearth over all the land of Egypt and Chanaan, and great affliction: and our fathers found no sustenance” (Act 7:11) — the emptiness that drove Jacob's sons to the brother they had sold. Supplied: when David fled from Absalom, an old man met him at Mahanaim, “Barzillai was a very aged man, even fourscore years old: and he had provided the king of sustenance while he lay at Mahanaim; for he was a very great man” (2Sa 19:32). He fed a king in exile when it was dangerous to be seen doing it, and afterwards refused the reward. And asked for: the Lord teaches His disciples to pray, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Mat 6:11) — sustenance, requested daily, from a Father who knows what we have need of before we ask.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sustenance as support; maintenance; subsistence; that which supports life; food; victuals; provisions.
webster_full: SUS'TENANCE, n. Support; maintenance; subsistence; as, the sustenance of the body.
2. That which supports life; food; victuals; provisions.
SUSTA'IN, v.t. To bear; to uphold; to support; to keep from sinking in ruin or in want.
DEARTH, n. Scarcity; want; especially of provisions; famine.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 19:32
Now Barzillai was a very aged man, even fourscore years old: and he had provided the king of sustenance while he lay at Mahanaim; for he was a very great man.
Judges 6:4
And they encamped against them, and destroyed the increase of the earth, till thou come unto Gaza, and left no sustenance for Israel, neither sheep, nor ox, nor ass.
Acts 7:11
Now there came a dearth over all the land of Egypt and Chanaan, and great affliction: and our fathers found no sustenance.
Matthew 6:11
Give us this day our daily bread.
corruption_summary: Daily dependence is engineered out of life, and the prayer for bread becomes a formality repeated by people who cannot remember needing it answered.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the daily in daily bread. Israel gathered manna one morning at a time and what was kept overnight bred worms; the Lord taught His church to ask for today's supply today. A society with full stores and long supply chains finds this petition hard to pray honestly, and the difficulty is worth admitting rather than covering. The remedy is not to manufacture insecurity but to remember, deliberately and often, that the harvest, the health, the work and the peace that stand behind a full table are all gifts, and that Judges 6 describes how quickly they can be taken.

Barzillai deserves to be remembered by name, and Scripture clearly intends that he should be. He was eighty years old and very great, and he provisioned a fugitive king at Mahanaim when David's cause looked finished and Absalom sat in Jerusalem. Afterwards, offered a place at the king's table for the rest of his life, he declined it and asked only to die in his own city near the graves of his father and mother, sending a younger man in his place. David remembered him on his deathbed and charged Solomon to show kindness to his sons. That is what sustenance given at the right hour is worth, and it is why the Lord will say, I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat.

Hebrew kalkal (H3557) — to contain, sustain, provide for; 2 Samuel 19:32, 1 Kings 17:4 of the ravens feeding Elijah.
Greek chortasma (G5527) — food, sustenance; Acts 7:11, its only occurrence.
Greek epiousios (G1967) — daily, for the coming day; Matthew 6:11 and Luke 11:3 only.
Exodus 16 fixes the pattern: manna gathered a day at a time, and what was hoarded bred worms.
usage: “He had provided the king of sustenance while he lay at Mahanaim” — and refused the reward.
“Left no sustenance for Israel, neither sheep, nor ox, nor ass”.
“Give us this day our daily bread” — today's supply, asked for today.

pos: n. (the Holiest of all; the inner sanctuary behind the second veil — Greek hagia hagion)
etymology: The superlative of holy, rendering the Hebrew idiom holy of holies — the Semitic way of forming a superlative by doubling the noun.
biblical_def: The Holiest is the innermost room of the sanctuary, and the epistle to the Hebrews is built around who may enter it. “After the second veil, the tabernacle which is called the Holiest of all” (Heb 9:3) — behind that veil stood the ark, and into it the high priest went alone, once a year, not without blood. The writer draws the lesson the arrangement was designed to teach: “The Holy Ghost this signifying, that the way into the holiest of all was not yet made manifest, while as the first tabernacle was yet standing” (Heb 9:8). The closed veil was itself a sermon: access was not yet open, and the annual repetition proved that nothing had been finished. Then the conclusion the whole epistle exists to reach: “Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh” (Heb 10:19-20). Every term is deliberate. Boldness, where once there was exclusion; to enter, and not merely to approach; by the blood of Jesus, and by nothing else; a way that is new and living, because the Priest who opened it is alive; and the veil is His flesh, torn from the top down when He died.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the holy of holies as the innermost apartment of the Jewish tabernacle and temple, where the ark was kept, and into which the high priest alone entered once a year.
webster_full: HO'LIEST, a. superlative of holy; most holy.
HOLY OF HOLIES, the innermost apartment of the Jewish tabernacle and temple, called also the most holy place.
VEIL, n. A cover; a curtain; in the temple, the hanging that separated the holy place from the most holy.
BOLD'NESS, n. Confidence; courage; liberty of access and of speech.
scriptures: Hebrews 10:19
Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus,
Hebrews 10:20
By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh;
Hebrews 9:3
And after the second veil, the tabernacle which is called the Holiest of all;
Hebrews 9:8
The Holy Ghost this signifying, that the way into the holiest of all was not yet made manifest, while as the first tabernacle was yet standing:
corruption_summary: A human priesthood is reintroduced between the believer and God, or else access is assumed on terms other than the blood, and both empty the torn veil of meaning.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 10:19 is the death of every sacerdotal system. The boldness to enter the holiest belongs to brethren — the whole company of believers — and the ground is the blood of Jesus, offered once. Where a church interposes a mediating priesthood, repeats a sacrifice, or makes access depend on a man's absolution, it has rebuilt the veil that God tore from the top downward at the ninth hour. Hebrews argues the point at length: those priests were many because death forbade them to continue, and they offered daily because nothing was ever finished; this Man, after He had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down.

The opposite error assumes access without reckoning what it cost. Nothing in these chapters supports a casual approach; the same epistle says our God is a consuming fire, and the boldness it grants is granted with the price named in the same sentence — by the blood of Jesus, through a veil that is His flesh. A worshipper who has understood Hebrews 9 comes into the holiest with confidence and with awe together, and the two are not in competition. He enters where the high priest trembled to go once a year, and he enters because Another went in first and did not come out to repeat it.
roots_summary: Greek hagia hagion, holy of holies — Hebrews 9:3; ta hagia, the holy places — Hebrews 9:8, 10:19; Hebrew qodesh haqqodashim, the most holy place; parresia (G3954), boldness of access.
