Greek parresia (G3954) — boldness, freedom of speech and access; Hebrews 10:19, Ephesians 3:12, 1 John 4:17.
Greek prosphatos (G4372) — new, freshly slain; Hebrews 10:20, the new and living way.
Hebrew qodesh haqqodashim — the most holy place; Exodus 26:33-34, entered once a year with blood.
Matthew 27:51 records the veil of the temple rent in twain from the top to the bottom at the moment He died.
usage: “Boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus” — addressed to brethren.
“The way into the holiest of all was not yet made manifest” — the closed veil preached.
“Through the veil, that is to say, his flesh”.

pos: adj. (external; in the Gospels, of the darkness outside the lighted hall — Greek exoteros)
etymology: A comparative of out. The Greek exoteros is the comparative of exo, outside — the region further out than where the light and the feast are.
biblical_def: Outer in the Gospels belongs to one terrible phrase, spoken three times by the Lord Jesus, always with the same clause attached. To those who presumed on descent: “the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Mat 8:12). To the man without a wedding garment: “Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Mat 22:13). To the servant who buried his talent: “cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Mat 25:30). Three men — one presuming on birth, one presuming on presence at the feast, one doing nothing with what he was given — and one destination. The image is of an eastern night: inside, a lighted hall and a wedding; outside the door, absolute dark. Hell in these sayings is exclusion from a joy that is going on. The word has its plain use elsewhere: at Ezekiel's vision, “the sound of the cherubims' wings was heard even to the outer court, as the voice of the Almighty God when he speaketh” (Eze 10:5) — a sound from the innermost place carrying out to the furthest, at the very hour the glory was departing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines outer as being on the outside; external; opposed to inner; as the outer court of the temple.
webster_full: OUT'ER, a. Being on the outside; external; opposed to inner; as the outer wall.
OUT'ERMOST, a. Being on the extreme external part.
DARK'NESS, n. Absence of light; a state of privation; in Scripture, a state of misery and exclusion from the presence of God.
GNASH, v.i. To strike the teeth together, as in anger or pain.
scriptures: Matthew 8:12
But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
Matthew 22:13
Then said the king to the servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
Matthew 25:30
And cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
Ezekiel 10:5
And the sound of the cherubims' wings was heard even to the outer court, as the voice of the Almighty God when he speaketh.
corruption_summary: Eternal punishment is denied outright, or reduced to a metaphor for self-chosen distance, and the Lord's own repeated words are the first casualty.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine of hell is not an invention of later theology; the sayings about outer darkness are the Lord's own, recorded three times in one Gospel, each time with weeping and gnashing of teeth attached. Annihilationism cannot account for the weeping, which requires someone to weep; universalism cannot account for the casting out, which is an act done to a person by a king's command; and the softer proposal that hell is merely a door locked from the inside cannot account for the binding hand and foot in Matthew 22:13. Whatever consolations Scripture gives — and it gives many — they are not to be purchased by deleting Christ's words.

The three occurrences are worth reading together for whom they name. The first is a Jew presuming on descent from Abraham; the second is a guest at the wedding without the garment the king supplied; the third is a servant of the household who simply did nothing with what he had been given. Not one of them is an obvious outsider. All three were, in some sense, inside the arrangement, and that is exactly the Lord's point in telling them to the people He told them to. The parables were spoken to men who assumed their place was secure, and the outer darkness in each is the loss of a place they had counted on.
roots_summary: Greek exoteros (G1857), outer, further out — Matthew 8:12, 22:13, 25:30 only; skotos (G4655), darkness; brugmos (G1030), a gnashing.
roots_lines: Greek exoteros (G1857) — outer, the region further outside; Matthew 8:12, 22:13 and 25:30, its only occurrences.
Greek skotos (G4655) — darkness; the noun joined to it in all three sayings.
Greek brugmos (G1030) — a grinding or gnashing of teeth; seven times in the Gospels, always of the same condition.
Hebrew chitson (H2435) — outer, external; Ezekiel 10:5 of the outer court.
All three sayings are addressed to men who assumed they were inside.
usage: “Cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” — three times, one clause.
“Bind him hand and foot” — not a door locked from the inside.
“The sound… was heard even to the outer court” — and the glory was departing.

pos: n. (one who breaks; in Micah, the One who breaks open the way — Hebrew parats)
etymology: From break, Old English brecan. The Hebrew parats means to burst through a wall or a fold — the word used of a breach in a city and of a flock forcing an opening.
biblical_def: Breaker in Micah is a title, and one of the most striking pictures of Christ in the prophets. The chapter has just promised a gathering: “I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as the flock in the midst of their fold” (Mic 2:12). Then the deliverance: “The breaker is come up before them: they have broken up, and have passed through the gate, and are gone out by it: and their king shall pass before them, and the LORD on the head of them” (Mic 2:13). The image is a penned flock and one who goes up ahead of them and bursts the wall of the fold, so that the sheep pour out through the gap He made, with their king at their head. He goes first; they follow through the opening; the LORD leads them out. Every deliverance of God's people has that shape, and it is finally fulfilled in the One who said, “I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture” (Joh 10:9). The word has its other, plainer use in Paul: “circumcision verily profiteth, if thou keep the law: but if thou be a breaker of the law, thy circumcision is made uncircumcision” (Rom 2:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a breaker as one who breaks; a violator; a transgressor; and also a wave broken by rocks or the shore.
webster_full: BREAK'ER, n. One who breaks; a violator; a transgressor; as, a breaker of the law.
2. A wave broken by rocks or a sand bank; a surge.
BREACH, n. The act of breaking; a gap or opening made by breaking; as a breach in a wall.
FOLD, n. A pen or inclosure for sheep; a place where a flock of sheep is kept.
scriptures: Micah 2:13
The breaker is come up before them: they have broken up, and have passed through the gate, and are gone out by it: and their king shall pass before them, and the LORD on the head of them.
Micah 2:12

I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as the flock in the midst of their fold: they shall make great noise by reason of the multitude of men.
John 10:9
I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture.
Romans 2:25
For circumcision verily profiteth, if thou keep the law: but if thou be a breaker of the law, thy circumcision is made uncircumcision.
corruption_summary: Deliverance is expected without a deliverer going first, and religious standing is trusted while the law it belongs to is broken.
corruption_paragraphs: Micah 2:13 will not permit a self-help account of salvation. The flock is penned; the wall does not fall on its own; someone goes up before them and bursts it, and only then do they pass through the gate and go out by it. The order in the verse is fixed: the breaker first, the people after, the King at their head. Every scheme in which men break themselves out — by resolve, by ritual, by improvement — has replaced the first clause. And the last clause is worth its own weight: the LORD on the head of them. They do not go out to find their way; they go out behind Him.

Romans 2:25 applies the other sense of the word to the very people who had the covenant sign. Circumcision profits if the law is kept; if a man is a breaker of the law, his circumcision is made uncircumcision. Paul is telling men with the mark that the mark does not hold when the thing it signified is abandoned. The parallel in a Christian congregation is exact and uncomfortable: baptism, membership, attendance and orthodoxy are real and are not nothing, and none of them survives as evidence in a man who lives in settled disobedience. The sign points to a reality; where the reality is absent the sign witnesses against him.

Hebrew porets — the participle, the breaker; Micah 2:13, used as a title.
Greek parabates (G3848) — a transgressor, one who steps across; Romans 2:25, James 2:11.
The picture is a sheepfold with a wall burst open from the outside, and the flock pouring through the gap.
Micah 2:13 ends with two leaders in one line: their king shall pass before them, and the LORD on the head of them.
usage: “The breaker is come up before them” — the wall does not fall on its own.
“The LORD on the head of them” — they go out behind Him.
“If thou be a breaker of the law, thy circumcision is made uncircumcision”.

pos: n. (dominion, victory; the contest of the games — Greek agonizomai, to strive in the arena)
etymology: From master, Latin magister. In 1 Corinthians 9:25 the phrase striveth for the mastery renders a single Greek verb drawn from the athletic contests.
biblical_def: Mastery is dominion won in a contest, and Paul takes the word from the games: “every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible” (1Co 9:25). He is arguing from what everyone in Corinth had seen at the Isthmian games. An athlete in training governs his sleep, his food, and his company, not because those things are wicked but because he is after a prize; and he does it for a wreath that withers. Paul applies it to himself without flinching: “I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway” (1Co 9:27). The word appears elsewhere in its plain senses. On the mountain Moses corrects Joshua's reading of the noise below: “It is not the voice of them that shout for mastery, neither is it the voice of them that cry for being overcome: but the noise of them that sing do I hear” (Exo 32:18) — not a battle, but a revel around a calf. And in the lions' den, of Daniel's accusers: “the lions had the mastery of them, and brake all their bones in pieces or ever they came at the bottom of the den” (Dan 6:24), the same lions that had not touched Daniel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mastery as dominion; power of command; superiority; pre-eminence; victory in war or in a contest.
webster_full: MAS'TERY, n. Dominion; power of governing or commanding.
2. Superiority in competition; preeminence; victory in war or in a contest.
3. Superior dexterity; superior skill; as, to obtain the mastery of an art.
TEM'PERATE, a. Moderate; not excessive; governing the appetites and passions.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 9:25
And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.
1 Corinthians 9:27
But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.
Exodus 32:18
And he said, It is not the voice of them that shout for mastery, neither is it the voice of them that cry for being overcome: but the noise of them that sing do I hear.
Daniel 6:24

And the king commanded, and they brought those men which had accused Daniel, and they cast them into the den of lions, them, their children, and their wives; and the lions had the mastery of them, and brake all their bones in pieces or ever they came at the bottom of the den.
corruption_summary: Discipline of the body is dismissed as legalism, and Paul's own practice — keeping under his body lest he be a castaway — is explained away rather than imitated.
corruption_paragraphs: A generation that has rightly learned that works do not justify has often wrongly concluded that effort is suspect. First Corinthians 9 is written by the apostle of justification by faith, and it is full of running, striving, buffeting and subjection. The distinction is not difficult: no exertion earns a standing before God, and no man who has that standing is thereby excused from training. Paul draws his illustration from athletes who were temperate in all things for a wreath that browned in a week, and asks the obvious question about a crown that does not fade. Where self-denial is treated as legalism by definition, the church loses the very vocabulary this chapter supplies.

Verse 27 is the sharpest and the most argued over: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway. It does not teach that a true believer may perish, which the same apostle denies at length in Romans 8; it teaches that the means by which God keeps His people include their striving, and that a preacher is not exempt from the warnings he administers. The doctrine of perseverance is a doctrine of perseverance — the saints are kept, and they are kept persevering. A man who reasons from his security to his slackness has not understood the security.
roots_summary: Greek agonizomai (G75), to contend in the games, strive for the mastery — 1 Corinthians 9:25, Colossians 1:29, 1 Timothy 6:12; enkrateuomai (G1467), to be temperate; Hebrew gaburah (H1369), might, mastery.
roots_lines: Greek agonizomai (G75) — to strive as in the arena; 1 Corinthians 9:25, Luke 13:24, Colossians 4:12 of Epaphras labouring fervently in prayer.
Greek enkrateuomai (G1467) — to exercise self-control, be temperate; 1 Corinthians 9:25 and 7:9.
Greek adokimos (G96) — disapproved, castaway; 1 Corinthians 9:27, the athlete disqualified.
Hebrew gaburah (H1369) — might, mastery; Exodus 32:18, of the shout of the strong.
The Isthmian games were held near Corinth, so Paul's readers knew exactly what training he meant.
usage: “Every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things”.
“They do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible”.
“The lions had the mastery of them” — the same lions that had not touched Daniel.

pos: adj. and adv. (four times the amount; the restitution the law required for a stolen sheep — Hebrew arbatayim)
etymology: From four and fold, in the sense of times. The word belongs to the law of restitution, where the multiple was fixed according to the offence.
biblical_def: Fourfold is a legal quantity before it is anything else. The law of Moses fixed it: “If a man shall steal an ox, or a sheep, and kill it, or sell it; he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep” (Exo 22:1). So when Nathan told David the parable of the rich man who took the poor man's one ewe lamb, David pronounced sentence out of the statute: “he shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity” (2Sa 12:6) — and had just sentenced himself, and lost four sons. The word's great moment is at Jericho. “Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord; Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold” (Luk 19:8). A chief publican, whose whole fortune came from exaction, volunteers the maximum penalty of the law against himself — not a percentage, not an apology, but the thief's restitution, and half his estate besides. The Lord's verdict follows: “This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham” (Luk 19:9). The restitution did not buy the salvation; it proved that salvation had arrived.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fourfold as four double; quadruple; four times told; as, to restore fourfold.
webster_full: FOURFOLD, a. Four double; quadruple; four times told; as a fourfold division.
FOURFOLD, adv. In fourfold measure; as, he shall restore the lamb fourfold.
RESTITU'TION, n. The act of returning or restoring to a person some thing or right of which he has been unjustly deprived.
PUB'LICAN, n. A collector of the Roman revenue; a farmer of the taxes, held in odium among the Jews.
scriptures: Luke 19:8
And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord; Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold.
2 Samuel 12:6
And he shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity.
Exodus 22:1
If a man shall steal an ox, or a sheep, and kill it, or sell it; he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep.
Luke 19:9
And Jesus said unto him, This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham.
corruption_summary: Repentance is reduced to sorrow expressed, with no restitution attached, and where restitution is required it is mistaken for the price of forgiveness.
corruption_paragraphs: Zacchaeus sets the standard that most modern repentance never reaches. He did not apologize; he calculated. Half of his goods to the poor, and fourfold to anyone he had defrauded — the heaviest restitution the law knew, applied by the offender to himself, in public, without being asked. Where a church accepts sorrow and a form of words as sufficient evidence of repentance in matters of theft, fraud or slander, it is asking less than a tax collector volunteered on the day he was converted. John the Baptist told the publicans the same thing in fewer words: exact no more than that which is appointed you.

The order in the passage must be kept exactly, or the whole scene becomes moralism. Christ called Zacchaeus down from the tree, invited Himself to the house, and was received joyfully — and the crowd murmured that He had gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner — and then Zacchaeus stood and made his restitution. The Lord's answer, this day is salvation come to this house, is a declaration about what had already happened, of which the fourfold restoration was the fruit. Nathan's parable shows the reverse case for warning: David pronounced the fourfold sentence readily on another man and did not see himself until the prophet said, Thou art the man.
roots_summary: Hebrew arbatayim (H706), fourfold — 2 Samuel 12:6; Greek tetraplous (G5073), fourfold — Luke 19:8 only; shalam (H7999), to make restitution, make whole.
roots_lines: Hebrew arbatayim (H706) — fourfold; 2 Samuel 12:6, its only occurrence.
Greek tetraplous (G5073) — fourfold; Luke 19:8, its only occurrence in the New Testament.
Hebrew shalam (H7999) — to make whole, restore, repay; the verb of the restitution laws, from the root of shalom.
Exodus 22:1 fixes the multiples: five oxen for an ox, four sheep for a sheep.
Leviticus 6:5 adds the fifth part for a man who confesses his own fraud, which is the lighter penalty Zacchaeus declined.
usage: “I restore him fourfold” — volunteered, in public, unasked.
“He shall restore the lamb fourfold” — and David had sentenced himself.
“This day is salvation come to this house” — the verdict, after which the fruit.
